sections.heading: Introduction to Databases
sections.content: A database is an organised collection of interrelated data stored and accessed electronically. A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that manages databases. MySQL is a popular open-source Relational DBMS (RDBMS).
keyPoints: Database: organised collection of structured data
DBMS: software for creating, managing, and accessing databases
RDBMS stores data in tables (relations) with rows and columns
MySQL is a free, open-source RDBMS widely used in web applications
Key terms: Table, Row (Record/Tuple), Column (Field/Attribute), Primary Key, Foreign Key

sections.heading: SQL — Data Definition and Manipulation
sections.content: SQL (Structured Query Language) is used to communicate with a database. It is divided into DDL (Data Definition Language) and DML (Data Manipulation Language).
keyPoints: DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP — define database structure
DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT — manipulate data
DCL: GRANT, REVOKE — control access permissions
TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK — transaction control
SQL is case-insensitive for keywords

codeExample.explanation: The CREATE TABLE statement defines the schema. INSERT adds rows. SELECT retrieves data. UPDATE modifies existing rows. DELETE removes rows.

sections.heading: SELECT Queries — Filtering and Sorting
sections.content: The SELECT statement is the most commonly tested SQL command in CBSE exams. It retrieves data based on conditions using WHERE, orders results using ORDER BY, groups using GROUP BY, and filters groups using HAVING.
keyPoints: SELECT column1, column2 FROM table WHERE condition
WHERE: filter rows — uses =, !=, >, <, >=, <=, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL
ORDER BY: sort results — ASC (default) or DESC
GROUP BY: aggregate data by one or more columns
HAVING: filter grouped results (like WHERE but for groups)
DISTINCT: remove duplicate rows
Aggregate functions: COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MAX(), MIN()

codeExample.explanation: WHERE filters before grouping; HAVING filters after grouping. This distinction is critical for CBSE board answers.

sections.heading: Joins — Combining Tables
sections.content: A JOIN clause is used to combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column. The CBSE syllabus covers Cartesian Product (Cross Join) and Equi-Join (Inner Join).
keyPoints: Cartesian Product: combines every row of table A with every row of table B — result has m×n rows
Equi-Join (Inner Join): joins tables where values in a column are equal
Natural Join: equi-join that removes duplicate columns
Foreign Key links two tables — common join condition
Syntax: SELECT … FROM TableA, TableB WHERE TableA.col = TableB.col

codeExample.explanation: The REFERENCES keyword defines a foreign key. Both join syntaxes are expected in CBSE answers.

sections.heading: Previous Year Questions
sections.content: SQL questions typically ask you to write queries for given scenarios, often involving a specific table structure. Practice writing SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and JOIN queries.
keyPoints: 2023: Write SQL to display all students scoring more than 80 marks, sorted by name
2022: Write SQL to find the count of students in each class
2021: Write SQL to join Student and Teacher tables to display class teacher name
2020: Identify primary key and foreign key from given table structure
Common mistake: using HAVING without GROUP BY
Common mistake: forgetting semicolon at end of queries in exam
